result.summary: Pindar's ode for Midas of Akragas, a victor in the flute-playing contest at Pytho, begins with a prayer to the city of Akragas to welcome the crown. It then tells how Perseus slew Medusa and how Athena invented flute music from the Gorgon's lament. It ends with a reflection that human success needs toil and that fortune is unpredictable.

scenes.title: Editor's introductory notes
scenes.summary: A note dates the victory to 494 or 450 and explains that the ode was probably sung in a procession at Akragas.

scenes.title: Prayer to Akragas
scenes.summary: The poet asks the city of Akragas to welcome the victory crown from Pytho and the flute-player Midas who won it.

scenes.title: Perseus slays Medusa
scenes.summary: Perseus kills Medusa and blinds the children of Phorkos, then brings her head to Seriphos for Polydektes' wedding. Athena hears the Gorgon's lament and makes the flute.
scenes.stakes: Perseus risks death in facing the Gorgons and must rescue his mother from Polydektes' mistreatment.

scenes.title: Athena's gift of the flute
scenes.summary: Athena gives the flute to mortals and names its tune the many-headed air, played by the reeds of Kephisos' nymph near the city of the Graces.

scenes.title: Reflection on fortune
scenes.summary: Pindar says happiness comes only with labour, and that time brings unexpected gains.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet for Athena as the virgin goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable closing maxim that happiness needs toil and fortune is unforeseeable.

analysis.text: The ode links victory in music to the hero's labour: art arises from suffering, and success follows toil.
Pindar celebrates a flute victory, showing that musical contests at the Pythian games were honoured like athletic ones.

fun_facts.text: Pythian 12 is the only surviving victory ode for an aulos (flute) player rather than an athlete.

language_notes.text: Pytho is the older name of Delphi, where the Pythian Games were held; the crown is the victor's wreath.
"Tutelar"-style address aside, "haunt of Persephone" refers to Sicily, a land sacred to Persephone; "inhabitest" and "nourisheth" are archaic second- and third-person verb forms.
The third sister is Medusa, the mortal one of the three Gorgons; her death caused the lament Athena heard.
"Bare thence their doom" means Perseus carried Medusa's head to Seriphos, bringing ruin to its people through its petrifying power.
Polydektes, king of Seriphos, tried to force Perseus' mother Danaë into marriage; Perseus' gift of the Gorgon's head turned him to stone.
Zeus visited Danaë as a shower of gold, hence Perseus is said to be sprung from a stream of gold.
"The Maiden" is Athena, called Pallas Athene earlier; Euryale is one of the two immortal Gorgon sisters, mourning Medusa.
The "many-headed air" is a flute melody whose name recalls the Gorgons' snaky heads; it may also refer to a many-parted tune.
"The thing ordained is not avoidable" means what fate has fixed cannot be escaped; "unaware" means unexpectedly.

context_notes.text: Pindar's Pythian Games victories were won at Delphi; the ode honours a flute-player, unusual since most victors were athletes.
Akragas (Agrigentum) was a wealthy Greek city in Sicily, famous for its grand temples.
The Graces' city is Orchomenos in Boeotia, near the river Kephisos; the Graces were goddesses of charm and beauty.

literary_notes.text: The poet directly addresses the city as a queen, treating Akragas as a divine, personified being who can receive the crown.
Serpent heads and anguished pouring sound make the Gorgon's death vivid, linking horror to the origin of music.
"Grievous" is repeated to stress the harm Perseus' gift brought upon Polydektes.
The reeds and dancing-ground are called faithful witnesses, giving place and instrument a human role in honouring the music.
The closing general truth about labour and time turns the myth into a moral about fortune and hope.
